front: We provide our supplier, free of charge, a mold for making our parts. What is the mold called in valuation, and how is it treated?
back: An **assist**. Its value is added to the customs value, apportioned over the shipments made with it, although it appears on neither the invoice nor the PO.
extra: The classic BSA data gap: assists are often recorded nowhere, so a value built from purchase prices is too low. The apportionment method must be reasonable and applied consistently; the Senior agrees it with the broker.
reuses: Why are assists a data risk for a BSA?

front: How is a commission we pay our own buying agent treated in transaction value, compared with a selling commission paid by the buyer?
back: A **buying commission** is not added. A **selling commission** paid by the buyer is one of the five additions. The same holds in the US, Canada and Mexico.
extra: Check who the agent works for: our own agent (buying) or the seller's (selling). The five additions are added only if they are not already in the price.

front: Price US$10,000 FOB. We pay freight 800, insurance 50, buying commission 200, and supplied a mold free (1,000 apportioned). Customs value in US, Canada, Mexico?
back: **US and Canada: 11,000** (price + mold assist). **Mexico: 11,850**: it also adds freight and insurance up to arrival. The buying commission is added nowhere.
extra: US and Canada are FOB-like, Mexico is CIF-like. Transaction value is the first of six valuation methods; almost all our imports should use it, and the others apply, in order, only when it cannot.
reuses: Which of the three countries values imports on a CIF basis?

front: Our landed-cost model converts at Finance's planning exchange rate. Why will its duty differ slightly from the duty the broker files?
back: The broker converts at the rate each country fixes for a set date (US: the certified rate for the **date of exportation**). The model's planning rate differs, so a small gap is expected and should be explainable in PPV.
extra: Canada uses the Bank of Canada rate for the date of direct shipment; Mexico generally the rate for the date of entry. When model and filed duty differ slightly, check the conversion rate and date first.

front: What are the four ways a good can be USMCA-originating?
back: Origin criteria (Art. 4.2): **A** wholly obtained or produced in the region; **B** meets the product-specific rule; **C** made exclusively from originating materials; **D** a narrow case decided by an RVC test.
extra: A good with any non-originating material can only use B (or the narrow D). The criterion goes on the certification as data element 7.
reuses: What are the four USMCA origin criteria (A to D)?

front: A product-specific rule reads 'a change to heading 84.AA from any other heading'. What must be true of each non-originating material?
back: It must be classified in a **different heading** (4 digits) from the good: a tariff shift. A non-originating material already in 84.AA fails, unless de minimis covers it.
extra: Look the rule up by the finished good's HS code. A change of chapter compares 2 digits, a change of subheading 6. Read 'except from heading Y' clauses carefully. Originating materials do not need to shift.
reuses: What is a tariff shift rule of origin?

front: Pump PK-100 (TV US$211) fails the change of heading only because its US$25 non-originating housing shares the pump's heading. What does de minimis show?
back: **25 / 211 = 11.8%**, over the 10% limit, so the tariff shift still fails. Next, test the rule's alternative: regional value content.
extra: At a housing cost of US$14 (TV US$200), 14 / 200 = 7.0%: de minimis would save the shift and the pump would qualify under criterion B. De minimis compares the failing materials with the good's transaction value or total cost (Art. 4.12).
reuses: What is the USMCA de minimis rule?

front: Fictional rule: RVC at least 60% (transaction value) or 50% (net cost). PK-100: TV 211, net cost 185, VNM 89 (US$). Which method qualifies?
back: **Net cost:** (185 − 89) / 185 × 100 = **51.9%**, at least 50%. Transaction value gives (211 − 89) / 211 × 100 = 57.8%, under 60%, so it fails.
extra: Only the producer can calculate and support net cost, so the producer (or exporter) would normally certify. Real rules state their own methods and thresholds: read the rule, never assume one.
reuses: What is the USMCA net cost formula for regional value content (RVC)?

front: Retail set KT-200 (GRI 3(b)) is worth US$50; only its US$4 bit set is non-originating. How is its USMCA origin decided, and with what result?
back: By the **sets article** (Art. 4.17), not one product-specific rule: every good must originate, or the non-originating goods must be at most 10% of the set's value. 4 / 50 = **8%**: the set originates.
extra: If the bit set cost US$7 (set US$53): 7 / 53 = 13.2%, so the set fails unless the bit set itself originates. The article applies only when the kit is classified as a set; otherwise qualify each item separately.

front: Who may complete a USMCA certification of origin?
back: The **importer, exporter or producer** (USMCA Art. 5.2). If qualification rests on the producer's own cost data, such as net cost, the producer (or exporter) normally certifies.
extra: Mexico has accepted importer certifications since 1 January 2024. Do not confuse the certifier (who completes it) with the claimant: the importer always makes the preference claim.
reuses: Who may complete a USMCA certification of origin?

front: What form must a USMCA certification of origin use, and what must it contain?
back: **No set form**: any format, even on the invoice, works if it contains the **nine minimum data elements** of Annex 5-A. NAFTA's CBP Form 434 is no longer used.
extra: Review each supplier certification for all nine elements, the item match, the blanket period and the signature; reject incomplete ones. Element 7, the origin criterion (A to D), must match the qualification result.
reuses: What format must a USMCA certification of origin follow?

front: How long a period can one USMCA blanket certification cover for repeat shipments of identical goods?
back: **Up to 12 months**, stated on the certification. Start the next supplier request before it ends: an expired certification leaves the claim unsupported.
extra: Supplier solicitation tracks this. Useful measures: certifications expiring in the next 60 days, and claims filed without a certification on file (should be zero).
reuses: What period can a USMCA blanket certification cover?

front: How long must an importer keep the certification, BOM and calculation behind a USMCA claim?
back: At least **5 years after importation** (USMCA Art. 5.8); **6 in Canada**. Keep the certification, BOM and calculation, supplier certifications, cost data and proof of the transaction.
extra: Do not confuse it with the 4 years for which customs must accept a certification after it is completed. US import records in general: 5 years from entry (19 CFR 163.4); drawback records until 3 years after the drawback claim is liquidated.
reuses: How long must an importer claiming USMCA preference keep records?

front: A qualifying good entered the US without a USMCA claim. How long does the importer have to claim, and what does an approved claim refund?
back: **One year from importation**, by a post-importation claim (19 U.S.C. 1520(d)) with a certification. An approved claim refunds the excess duty **and the MPF** paid.
extra: Pub. L. 116-260 (2020) authorized the MPF refund, back to 1 July 2020; ignore older CBP guidance that says MPF is not refunded. CBP cannot extend the one-year deadline. At entry, the claim is SPI 'S' on the line.
reuses: How does a US importer claim USMCA preference after entry when it did not claim at entry?

front: CBP sends a Form 28 request for information about a USMCA claim. What must the BSA be able to produce, and what if it can't?
back: The item's **qualification file**, within days: certification, BOM and calculation, supplier certifications and origin information. Without that support the claim can be denied, with duties, interest and possibly penalties.
extra: Tell the Senior the same day and pull the data; the Senior, not you, replies to CBP and the broker. Build the file when the claim is made: rule text, who prepared, who checked, the date.

front: A press release and a fact sheet announce a new US tariff action. Which document actually governs its dates, scope and rates?
back: The **legal instrument**: the proclamation, executive order or notice. Press releases, fact sheets, news and law-firm or broker alerts are only leads: use them to find the instrument; when they differ, the instrument wins.
extra: Fact sheets have differed from the proclamation on rates and dates. Annexes can be posted later or corrected, and one action can come as several proclamations on the same day.

front: Which CBP publication tells filers the Chapter 99 numbers and reporting order for a new US action?
back: A **CBP CSMS message** (Cargo Systems Messaging Service). Read every follow-up message too: CBP corrects details, such as drawback treatment or exemption lines, in later messages.
extra: It often comes the day before or the day of effect, sometimes before the Federal Register. Cite it in the brief with the instrument. Daily monitoring starts with the CSMS folder.
reuses: Tariff action (US): where are the filing instructions for a new action published?

front: Where in the HTSUS does a new US additional duty get its own heading, reported on the entry line next to the normal code?
back: In **Chapter 99**, subchapter III (9903 headings). The 9903 number is reported **in addition to** the Chapter 1–97 classification, never instead of it.
extra: The 9903 number tells CBP which action, exemption or exclusion applies, and so which extra rate to charge. Some 9903 numbers mean 'not subject': reporting them claims the exemption. The HTSUS revision can lag the effective date.
reuses: What is the purpose of HTSUS Chapter 99?

front: What decides whether a new US duty applies to goods shipped before its effective date but entered after it?
back: The **entry**: goods entered for consumption (or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption) on or after the stated date and time pay it. PO, ship and receipt dates do not count, unless the action says otherwise, such as an in-transit provision.
extra: Quote the timing clause word for word, including the time and time zone (daylight or standard). Goods in a bonded warehouse take the rate in force when they are withdrawn (19 CFR 141.69).
reuses: Tariff action (US): which event usually decides whether a new duty applies to a shipment?

front: In a Tariff-Impact Brief, how do you record an action's timing, scope, exclusion and stacking wording?
back: **Quote, then interpret.** Paste the exact words first. Write 'our working interpretation' separately underneath, with a confidence level: High, Medium or Low.
extra: Medium or Low items that change scope, rate or date need broker or counsel confirmation, through the Senior, before release. A brief with an open Low item goes out only as 'provisional', with the Manager's approval.
source: Tariff-Impact Brief template, How to fill this in

front: A requester asks which items a new tariff action hits and what it does to our cost. How is the request set up in Jira?
back: As an **epic** with two linked stories: Research (the WHAT, in a Tariff-Impact Brief) and Standard Cost (the $, in the Tariff-Impact Model). The Research story **blocks** the Standard Cost story.
extra: The boundary rule in action: Standard Cost never decides scope; it computes $ on Research's determinations. Each story has its own maker and checker.

front: During intake triage, which conditions make a request P1?
back: Any one of: **Urgency 3 and Risk 3**; wrong data reaching a broker, Finance or a system **now**; or a regulatory effective date **within 10 working days** that may cover our items.
extra: Tell the Manager at once (within 30 minutes for a new tariff action). In days 1 to 60 the Manager confirms every P1 or P2 priority, and every decline, before you send it.

front: How should one requirement be written, and what does an 'and' inside it usually signal?
back: As **one testable sentence**: 'The [tool, report or process] shall [behavior] [condition].' An 'and' usually means two requirements: split them.
extra: Every Must also needs acceptance criteria a tester can check with real data, often as Given/When/Then. Give each requirement a source (person and date, regulation, defect); confirm or delete any without one.
source: Requirements template, How to fill this in

front: In a requirements document, how does a business rule differ from a requirement? Give a duty-rate example.
back: A **business rule** is true whatever the system: a US import pays the rate in effect at entry. A **requirement** says what the system does about it: 'The tool shall store an effective-from date for each rate.'
extra: Keep them in separate sections, each with a source. Rules on scope, rates and dates come from a checked Tariff-Impact Brief; cost rules, such as the costing reference date, come from Finance policy.
source: Requirements template, How to fill this in
